materials.title: Section II · Part A · Text 1材料
materials.text:
When a city introduced software to rank applications for emergency housing, officials expected complaints to decline. The previous process had been slow, and applicants rarely understood why one household moved ahead of another. The new system produced a short explanation for every score. Yet the number of challenges rose. Some administrators treated this as evidence that transparency had failed. A legal adviser offered a different interpretation: for the first time, people could identify which recorded fact they needed to correct. A rise in challenges might therefore indicate improved access to the process rather than poorer decisions.

The distinction matters because an explanation can serve several purposes. A technical account may help an engineer reproduce a score while leaving an applicant unable to act. Telling a family that its application was assigned a certain statistical weight reveals little if the family cannot inspect the underlying record. Conversely, a plain statement that an address was classified as temporary can create a practical opportunity to supply missing evidence. The useful question is thus not simply whether a system explains itself, but whether its explanation connects to a procedure through which an affected person can obtain a meaningful review.

There are limits to that procedure. A reviewer may correct an inaccurate address without questioning whether temporary accommodation should receive the assigned weight in the first place. Such policy choices require public justification, and they cannot be settled by presenting more detailed descriptions of computer operations. Nor does replacing technical vocabulary with everyday language automatically make a rule fair. A clearly explained rule can still distribute burdens in a way that citizens have good reasons to reject. Transparency creates a starting point for judgment; it does not provide a substitute for judgment or a guarantee of acceptable outcomes.

The city eventually changed its evaluation plan. Alongside processing time and the total number of appeals, it began recording how many applicants could correct relevant information, whether corrections altered outcomes, and which complaints concerned the policy itself. These measures did not produce a single attractive score for the annual report. They did, however, distinguish between administrative mistakes and disagreements about priorities. The adviser argued that this was precisely the point. A public explanation earns its value through the questions and actions it makes possible, even when those questions make an institution's performance look less comfortable in the short term. The new approach made institutional learning visible rather than effortless.

materials.title: Section II · Part A · Text 2材料
materials.text:
Predictions of the public library's disappearance usually begin with a familiar observation: many documents once available only on library shelves can now be read on a telephone. If the library is understood as a warehouse of scarce information, its future does look uncertain. But that understanding overlooks work that was always present and has recently become more visible. Librarians help people frame questions, judge the reliability of unfamiliar sources, and complete tasks whose difficulty lies less in locating information than in knowing what to do with it. Digital abundance has changed the setting of that work without removing its necessity.

A branch in a former industrial town illustrates the change. Its staff noticed that residents attending employment workshops could often find vacancies online but struggled with application systems. Some had no private place to make a video call; others could not tell whether a request for personal information was legitimate. The branch added reservable booths and short appointments with trained advisers. Book borrowing remained important, but it no longer described the full service. Simply counting loans would have made the branch's response to local needs appear unsuccessful at the very moment when more residents were relying on it.

This expanded role is not costless. Time spent helping one visitor navigate an application cannot be spent maintaining a collection or assisting another visitor. Libraries also risk becoming convenient substitutes for services that other public bodies should provide. When an employment agency closes its local office and sends everyone to the library, the transfer may arrive without money or specialist support. Staff who welcome new uses of their buildings therefore have good reason to ask who should fund them. Recognizing social value does not require pretending that every institution has unlimited capacity or that every responsibility can be shifted without consequences.

The strongest case for adaptation is consequently neither nostalgia for a quieter past nor enthusiasm for every new request. It is a claim about a continuing public function: helping people use knowledge under changing conditions. Decisions about space, staffing, and collections should follow evidence about that function in a particular community. A library may need more books in one district and more supported access to digital systems in another. Treating these choices as a contest between paper and screens misses the harder issue. What matters is whether the institution has the resources and judgment to make information usable for the people it serves. That requires attention to both public purpose and available resources.

materials.title: Section II · Part A · Text 3材料
materials.text:
A washing machine advertised as repairable may still be difficult to repair in practice. The case can be opened, its damaged part can be replaced, and the manufacturer may even publish a repair guide. Yet a local technician might wait months for a small component or discover that the required diagnostic tool is available only to an authorized chain. A design feature has then been mistaken for a complete service. Repairability is better understood as a relationship among products, information, parts, skills, and the time available to the person whose machine has stopped working.

This broader view changes how a repair label should be evaluated. A score based solely on the number of screws needed to remove a cover measures something real, but it may overlook a more decisive obstacle. Consumers need to know whether replacement parts remain available after a model has left the shops, whether their prices make repair reasonable, and whether independent technicians can obtain sufficient information. No label can include every circumstance. Nevertheless, selecting convenient measurements without considering how repairs actually occur risks rewarding products that look accessible on a test bench while remaining expensive to maintain at home.

Manufacturers offer several objections to wider access. Some diagnostic systems include safety controls, and poorly executed repairs can cause harm. These concerns deserve assessment rather than automatic dismissal. They do not, however, establish that every restriction is necessary. A requirement that a technician complete relevant safety training differs from a rule that permits only one commercial network to obtain a harmless error code. The important policy task is to identify a proportionate response to a specific risk. General references to safety should not end discussion of arrangements that also protect a company's profitable service business from competition.

For households, time is another crucial resource. Even an inexpensive part may arrive too late for a family that depends on one washing machine. A policy encouraging repair might therefore consider local stock, clear delivery commitments, and temporary replacement services alongside product construction. Such measures are less visible than a new label, but they address the reasons people replace equipment that could technically be fixed. The purpose is not to insist that every object must be repaired whatever the cost. It is to give a feasible option a fair chance before delay, uncertainty, or restricted access makes replacement the only practical decision. Feasibility must be examined throughout the whole process of repair.

materials.title: Section II · Part A · Text 4材料
materials.text:
When a research result fails to appear in a later study, public discussion often seeks a simple verdict. Either the original researchers were careless or the new team must have performed the experiment badly. Both explanations are possible, but the demand for an immediate winner can obscure a third possibility: the effect depends on conditions that neither study initially treated as important. A different population, measurement interval, or institutional setting may change the outcome. Investigating those conditions can contribute more knowledge than defending a celebrated conclusion or declaring an entire field unreliable after a single disagreement.

This does not make every failed replication informative by itself. A new study needs adequate statistical power, a clear account of its procedures, and measures suitable for the question. Without those features, disagreement may be difficult to interpret. Preregistering an analysis can help distinguish decisions made before seeing data from those made afterward, but registration is not a certificate of good judgment. An inappropriate measure remains inappropriate even when its use was announced in advance. Methodological tools are useful because they make reasoning inspectable, not because they release researchers from the responsibility to reason carefully about what they are measuring.

Incentives complicate the picture. Journals and employers often reward striking findings more readily than careful tests of existing ones. A scientist considering a replication must therefore compare its intellectual importance with its likely professional return. Appeals to individual virtue leave this calculation largely unchanged. Some institutions have begun funding coordinated replications and recognizing shared datasets, protocols, and negative results as research contributions. These changes cannot guarantee reliable knowledge, but they lower the personal cost of work that a community claims to value. What scientists are encouraged to do should be considered alongside what they are advised to do.

The most productive response to disagreement is therefore organized curiosity. Researchers can specify which differences between studies might matter, design tests that separate competing explanations, and state how the results would change their claims. Occasionally this process will expose an error; sometimes it will identify a narrow boundary around a useful effect. In either case, knowledge improves through making the uncertainty more precise. The goal of replication is not merely to preserve confidence or to dramatize its collapse. It is to establish what can be expected, under which conditions, and with how much reason for that expectation. A useful disagreement can clarify a claim instead of destroying it.

materials.title: Section II · Part B材料
materials.text:
(41) Mira
At a tutoring charity I helped to evaluate two very different questions. The trustees wanted to decide whether to offer a second term; a university partner wanted to know why some children retained new vocabulary. Both could use test results, but only the trustees needed to know the cost and availability of tutors. The team was about to adopt the measures from an earlier project because the forms were ready. We stopped and wrote down what would count as a reason to renew this particular offer. That exercise changed what we asked the staff to record.

(42) Dev
The returned questionnaires looked reassuring until we realised that every invitation had gone through the same advice portal. Residents who never managed to sign in could not tell us that the page was unusable. Sending another batch of invitations through the portal would have made the file larger without uncovering the problem. A librarian helped us reach people who sought advice elsewhere and pointed out that her visitors were not representative either. The comparison between those groups mattered more to me than the total number of replies.

(43) Leah
A course reported weak progress although its teaching method had worked in a pilot. The timetable showed that half the learners had missed the sessions in which the method was used. When the manager proposed scrapping the method, we could not tell her that it was effective; the evaluation had not established that. But accepting that the result was disappointing did not settle which part of the programme was at fault. An attendance record and a visit to a class helped us decide what a second trial would have to change.

(44) Owen
During a short trial, almost all the estimates suggested a benefit, but they told us very little about how large it might be or how long it would last. Some board members wanted an immediate permanent service; others read the same report as a reason to close it. I proposed extending the trial for one term within the existing budget and agreeing now what evidence the board would examine at the end. The question was not whether we could eliminate every uncertainty. It was how far the present evidence justified committing our resources.

(45) Inez
A year after a project ended, its summary tables were still on the shared drive. No one could explain why one school had been left out or why the measure had changed midway through the year. We could reproduce a calculation without knowing whether it was the right calculation to reproduce. For the next project I asked for a brief account of each material change, linked to the relevant version of the data. Personal records stayed protected, but the team taking over could understand the decisions instead of inheriting only the published totals.

materials.title: Section II · Part C材料
materials.text:
Public institutions increasingly use numerical targets to show that they are responding to demand. The appeal is understandable: a target is easy to communicate, and progress can be displayed in a simple chart. But the meaning of a number depends on the activity it represents and on the choices made while producing it. A shorter waiting list, for example, may result from faster service, a change in eligibility, or a decline in people's willingness to apply. These explanations are not interchangeable, even if the reported figure looks identical.

[46] When a measure becomes the principal basis for judging an organisation, staff may direct their attention toward what improves the measure rather than toward everything the organisation exists to achieve.

This possibility does not mean that measurement should be abandoned. Without records, problems may remain invisible, and decisions may depend on the confidence of the most powerful speaker. The alternative is to connect measures to a clear account of purpose.

[47] A useful evaluation combines the discipline of counting with an explanation of whose experience is represented, which important outcomes remain unmeasured, and why those omissions matter to the decision being made.

Such an account is easier to produce when people doing the work can question the categories used in a report. A receptionist may notice that an apparently completed case requires several further visits. A visitor may describe an obstacle that no existing category records.

[48] These observations are not substitutes for systematic evidence, but they can reveal where an apparently precise indicator no longer provides an adequate description of the service people actually receive.

Managers must also distinguish between a measure designed to support learning and one tied to rewards or penalties. The latter changes the incentives surrounding a report and may require stronger checks on how data are recorded.

[49] Publishing a result can make an institution more accountable only if readers have enough information to understand how the result was produced and what conclusions it can reasonably support.

Good reporting therefore requires a conversation between numerical summaries and practical knowledge. Neither can do the other's work completely. Together they can make differences visible and help identify which changes deserve closer investigation.

[50] The aim is not to replace judgment with a number, but to give judgment a clearer evidential basis while preserving the possibility of questioning both the evidence and the priorities behind it.

source.exact:
When a city introduced software to rank applications for emergency housing, officials expected complaints to decline. The previous process had been slow, and applicants rarely understood why one household moved ahead of another. The new system produced a short explanation for every score. Yet the number of challenges rose. Some administrators treated this as evidence that transparency had failed. A legal adviser offered a different interpretation: for the first time, people could identify which recorded fact they needed to correct. A rise in challenges might therefore indicate improved access to the process rather than poorer decisions.

The distinction matters because an explanation can serve several purposes. A technical account may help an engineer reproduce a score while leaving an applicant unable to act. Telling a family that its application was assigned a certain statistical weight reveals little if the family cannot inspect the underlying record. Conversely, a plain statement that an address was classified as temporary can create a practical opportunity to supply missing evidence. The useful question is thus not simply whether a system explains itself, but whether its explanation connects to a procedure through which an affected person can obtain a meaningful review.

There are limits to that procedure. A reviewer may correct an inaccurate address without questioning whether temporary accommodation should receive the assigned weight in the first place. Such policy choices require public justification, and they cannot be settled by presenting more detailed descriptions of computer operations. Nor does replacing technical vocabulary with everyday language automatically make a rule fair. A clearly explained rule can still distribute burdens in a way that citizens have good reasons to reject. Transparency creates a starting point for judgment; it does not provide a substitute for judgment or a guarantee of acceptable outcomes.

The city eventually changed its evaluation plan. Alongside processing time and the total number of appeals, it began recording how many applicants could correct relevant information, whether corrections altered outcomes, and which complaints concerned the policy itself. These measures did not produce a single attractive score for the annual report. They did, however, distinguish between administrative mistakes and disagreements about priorities. The adviser argued that this was precisely the point. A public explanation earns its value through the questions and actions it makes possible, even when those questions make an institution's performance look less comfortable in the short term. The new approach made institutional learning visible rather than effortless.

source.exact:
Predictions of the public library's disappearance usually begin with a familiar observation: many documents once available only on library shelves can now be read on a telephone. If the library is understood as a warehouse of scarce information, its future does look uncertain. But that understanding overlooks work that was always present and has recently become more visible. Librarians help people frame questions, judge the reliability of unfamiliar sources, and complete tasks whose difficulty lies less in locating information than in knowing what to do with it. Digital abundance has changed the setting of that work without removing its necessity.

A branch in a former industrial town illustrates the change. Its staff noticed that residents attending employment workshops could often find vacancies online but struggled with application systems. Some had no private place to make a video call; others could not tell whether a request for personal information was legitimate. The branch added reservable booths and short appointments with trained advisers. Book borrowing remained important, but it no longer described the full service. Simply counting loans would have made the branch's response to local needs appear unsuccessful at the very moment when more residents were relying on it.

This expanded role is not costless. Time spent helping one visitor navigate an application cannot be spent maintaining a collection or assisting another visitor. Libraries also risk becoming convenient substitutes for services that other public bodies should provide. When an employment agency closes its local office and sends everyone to the library, the transfer may arrive without money or specialist support. Staff who welcome new uses of their buildings therefore have good reason to ask who should fund them. Recognizing social value does not require pretending that every institution has unlimited capacity or that every responsibility can be shifted without consequences.

The strongest case for adaptation is consequently neither nostalgia for a quieter past nor enthusiasm for every new request. It is a claim about a continuing public function: helping people use knowledge under changing conditions. Decisions about space, staffing, and collections should follow evidence about that function in a particular community. A library may need more books in one district and more supported access to digital systems in another. Treating these choices as a contest between paper and screens misses the harder issue. What matters is whether the institution has the resources and judgment to make information usable for the people it serves. That requires attention to both public purpose and available resources.

source.title: Section II · Part A · Text 3材料
source.exact:
A washing machine advertised as repairable may still be difficult to repair in practice. The case can be opened, its damaged part can be replaced, and the manufacturer may even publish a repair guide. Yet a local technician might wait months for a small component or discover that the required diagnostic tool is available only to an authorized chain. A design feature has then been mistaken for a complete service. Repairability is better understood as a relationship among products, information, parts, skills, and the time available to the person whose machine has stopped working.

This broader view changes how a repair label should be evaluated. A score based solely on the number of screws needed to remove a cover measures something real, but it may overlook a more decisive obstacle. Consumers need to know whether replacement parts remain available after a model has left the shops, whether their prices make repair reasonable, and whether independent technicians can obtain sufficient information. No label can include every circumstance. Nevertheless, selecting convenient measurements without considering how repairs actually occur risks rewarding products that look accessible on a test bench while remaining expensive to maintain at home.

Manufacturers offer several objections to wider access. Some diagnostic systems include safety controls, and poorly executed repairs can cause harm. These concerns deserve assessment rather than automatic dismissal. They do not, however, establish that every restriction is necessary. A requirement that a technician complete relevant safety training differs from a rule that permits only one commercial network to obtain a harmless error code. The important policy task is to identify a proportionate response to a specific risk. General references to safety should not end discussion of arrangements that also protect a company's profitable service business from competition.

For households, time is another crucial resource. Even an inexpensive part may arrive too late for a family that depends on one washing machine. A policy encouraging repair might therefore consider local stock, clear delivery commitments, and temporary replacement services alongside product construction. Such measures are less visible than a new label, but they address the reasons people replace equipment that could technically be fixed. The purpose is not to insist that every object must be repaired whatever the cost. It is to give a feasible option a fair chance before delay, uncertainty, or restricted access makes replacement the only practical decision. Feasibility must be examined throughout the whole process of repair.

stimulus.text:
(41) Mira
At a tutoring charity I helped to evaluate two very different questions. The trustees wanted to decide whether to offer a second term; a university partner wanted to know why some children retained new vocabulary. Both could use test results, but only the trustees needed to know the cost and availability of tutors. The team was about to adopt the measures from an earlier project because the forms were ready. We stopped and wrote down what would count as a reason to renew this particular offer. That exercise changed what we asked the staff to record.

(42) Dev
The returned questionnaires looked reassuring until we realised that every invitation had gone through the same advice portal. Residents who never managed to sign in could not tell us that the page was unusable. Sending another batch of invitations through the portal would have made the file larger without uncovering the problem. A librarian helped us reach people who sought advice elsewhere and pointed out that her visitors were not representative either. The comparison between those groups mattered more to me than the total number of replies.

(43) Leah
A course reported weak progress although its teaching method had worked in a pilot. The timetable showed that half the learners had missed the sessions in which the method was used. When the manager proposed scrapping the method, we could not tell her that it was effective; the evaluation had not established that. But accepting that the result was disappointing did not settle which part of the programme was at fault. An attendance record and a visit to a class helped us decide what a second trial would have to change.

(44) Owen
During a short trial, almost all the estimates suggested a benefit, but they told us very little about how large it might be or how long it would last. Some board members wanted an immediate permanent service; others read the same report as a reason to close it. I proposed extending the trial for one term within the existing budget and agreeing now what evidence the board would examine at the end. questions.prompt: A drawing shows two students beside a pile of returned assignments. One copies only the final answers into a notebook. The other writes 'Why did this step fail?' beside a worked solution. Write an essay describing the drawing, explaining its message, and giving your comments.
questions.solution:
The drawing presents two different ways of responding to mistakes. Faced with returned assignments, one student copies the final answers, while the other asks why a particular step failed. The contrast suggests that collecting correct results is not the same as improving one's reasoning.
An answer can tell a learner where a calculation should end, but it may leave the original misunderstanding untouched. By examining the route to an error, a student can discover a false assumption, an omitted condition, or a procedure used in the wrong situation. That understanding can then be tested on a different problem. This process requires more effort than copying, yet it makes later work less dependent on outside correction.
In my view, a useful notebook should preserve selected attempts and explanations as well as results. Teachers can support this practice by giving specific feedback and allowing time for revision. Students, in turn, should treat a mistake as a question to investigate. The aim is neither to celebrate errors nor to hide them, but to learn enough from them to reason more reliably next time.
